title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza denies using AI to write Caine Prize-winning story
source_used: BBC News (own reporting, full text read)
key_facts: Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza denied using AI to write his short story 'The Blue Fighter', which won this year's Caine Prize for African Writing (GBP 10,000) a week earlier.
He posted on X: 'For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote The Blue Fighter.'

The denial answers an article in The Atlantic by Vauhini Vara, published on Sunday 11 Oct 2026, which said the AI-detection software Pangram showed the story was entirely AI-generated; the Atlantic piece ran in our 12 Oct 2026 edition.

Caine Prize chair Ellah Wakatama told the BBC she was shocked The Atlantic had not waited for a full investigation, and said Pangram was 'not yet tested'; the prize does not check submissions for AI, writers vouch their work is original.

The prize is carrying out an internal investigation: Kundizeza is to send documentation about his drafts, and talks continue with the judges and The Shallow Tales Review, which first published the story in 2025.

Vara told the BBC's Front Row that Pangram's internal research showed its assessments were rarely wrong, but she conceded no AI detector is 100% accurate, and that every earlier Caine Prize winning story she ran through it came out 100% human.
African writers say AI accusations are mostly aimed at non-white writers; Nigerian publisher Wale Lawal, founder of The Republic magazine, called the article 'crazy, racist and wildly unethical'.

Other prizes have had similar rows this year: the Commonwealth Short Story Prize (winner Jamir Nazir) and Thélyson Orélien's withdrawal from the Goncourt; the BBC notes AI detectors can wrongly flag human writing.
quote_evidence: Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using artificial intelligence (AI) to write his short story, which won this year's Caine Prize for African Writing.

His statement comes a week after he scooped the £10,000 ($13,000) award and a recent article in The Atlantic said AI-detection software Pangram had shown his work about a boy whose family falls on hard times was entirely AI generated.
Research has found that AI detectors can wrongly flag human writing as AI generated.
why_it_matters_hint: A major literary prize winner is accused by an AI detector of using AI, which he denies, raising doubts about detector reliability and fairness to African writers.
event_date: Denial and Front Row interviews on 12-13 Oct 2026; Atlantic article published Sunday 11 Oct 2026
notes: Follow-up of the Atlantic report we carried on 12 Oct 2026 (item 95, headline only then). The BBC story is the first full text. The claim that the story is AI-written is unproven and disputed.
